idiom_name: closures over the method's locals; class with #private fields for a named, reusable computation
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's closures, so nested functions or arrow functions over the method's locals are the direct realization and the compiler keeps the captured state typed; a closure is enough whenever the steps are private to the call. When the computation must be a named unit - tested in isolation, injected as a dependency, or reused - extract a class with #private fields and one public compute method: #private is hard privacy enforced at runtime, whereas TypeScript's private modifier is erased by the compiler and provides no runtime encapsulation.
pitfalls: TypeScript's private keyword is erased at compile time; use #private fields (or closures) when the extracted state must actually be hidden at runtime.
Downleveling to ES5 turns #private fields into WeakMap bookkeeping, adding runtime cost for legacy targets.
Closures capture the binding, so loop-created steps must be bound per iteration or they all observe the final value.
